quote: Auf wie viel Procent richtig sind nach dem heutigen Standpunkt der Wissenschaften (Geodaesie, [-A-] Astrono- mie, Physik) die Axiome der Geometrie?
english: To what percentage are the axioms of geometry correct, from the current standpoint of the sciences (geodesy, astronomy, physics)?
topic: Brief philosophical notes on how accurately the axioms of geometry hold empirically, on theories needing a point, on mathematical existence as freedom from contradiction (with examples of algebraic roots and surfaces of negative curvature), and on Lilienthal's flights refuting Helmholtz's claim about the maximum mass of flying birds.

triage.modern_statement: This is not a well-defined mathematical research problem. It is an empirical, philosophical question: within what measurement error do the axioms of Euclidean geometry (especially the parallel axiom, i.e. zero curvature) describe physical space, according to geodesy, astronomy and physics? Put in modern terms, it asks for observational bounds on the curvature of physical space, or on how far real space deviates from Euclidean geometry.
triage.answered_by: This is not a separate Hilbert problem. Different people have worked on the empirical question it raises. Gauss's survey of the Brocken–Hohehagen–Inselsberg triangle was later cited as experience showing that the parallel postulate is approximately correct. In 1900 Karl Schwarzschild gave a lecture 'Ueber das zulässige Krümmungsmaass des Raumes' (Vierteljahrsschrift der Astronomischen Gesellschaft 35, 337–347) on the curvature of space that astronomy allows. General relativity later made spatial geometry depend on matter. Today cosmology measures spatial curvature directly: Planck 2018 together with BAO data gives Ω_K = 0.001 ± 0.002, which is consistent with flat space. The note is closely related to Hilbert's empiricist view of geometry, which fed into his 6th problem (axiomatizing physics), but it is not itself one of the 23 problems.

evidence.claim: Gauss's measured triangle between Brocken, Hohehagen and Inselsberg had sides of roughly 69, 85 and 107 km.
Sartorius reports that Gauss held that experience, e.g. the angles of the Brocken–Hohehagen–Inselsberg triangle, shows the parallel postulate is approximately correct.
In 1900 Schwarzschild gave a lecture 'Ueber das zulässige Krümmungsmaass des Raumes' on how much curvature of space astronomy allows.
Bibliographic record: Schwarzschild, Vierteljahrsschrift der Astronomischen Gesellschaft 35 (1900): 337–347.
Hilbert's 6th problem grew out of his work on the foundations of geometry and its link to the empirical sciences.
Planck 2018 combined with BAO measurements constrains spatial curvature to Ω_K = 0.001 ± 0.002, consistent with a flat universe.

triage.why: The note asks for an empirical precision figure ('what percentage'), not a mathematical theorem, so it is a philosophical or physical question rather than a research problem. Its substance, how far physical space deviates from Euclidean geometry, has a clear history: Gauss's geodetic triangle, Schwarzschild's 1900 astronomical bounds on curvature, general relativity, and modern cosmological measurements of curvature (still an active area, e.g. Planck). I found no source that discusses this specific diary entry, so linking it to these works is my own reading of the topic, not a documented line of influence. Only the link to Hilbert's empiricist view of geometry and the 6th problem is backed by the historical literature.
